newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi to appeal after court rejects bias plea.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi to appeal after court rejects bias plea.

text.p: An Italian appeal court on Monday rejected a request by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi to remove a judge presiding over a trial in which the media tycoon is accused of corruption, judicial sources said.
But Berlusconi's lawyer said he intended to take the request for judge Carlo Crivelli to be dismissed on the grounds of bias to Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation.
Lawyer Ennio Amodio also told reporters: "Having read the decision of the appeal court closely, we will ask (Crivelli) to step down as presiding judge."

The Milan court of appeal ruled that while Crivelli had shown "a serious lapse in style for a presiding judge" and had damaged his credibility, no bias in favour of the prosecution was evident from remarks he made outside court proceedings.
It added, however, that under the circumstances it would have been better for Crivelli to have resigned "once a germ of doubt had been sown on the credibility of the proceedings."
Amodio told reporters the appeal court had taken note "of a serious and anomalous situation which affects the prestige and credibility of the judge.
"The court of appeal did not have the courage to take the definitive step, that is to establish that Crivelli should not continue to preside over this trial," Amodio said.
"But certainly the Court of Cassation will be able to examine this whole grave and anomalous situation," he said.

The trial, in which Berlusconi and his younger brother Paolo are accused of complicity in paying alleged bribes to tax inspectors, will continue with Crivelli presiding until a Court of Cassation decision, unless he himself now decides to resign.
Berlusconi, his younger brother Paolo, and two other defendants, lodged the original request for Crivelli's dismissal last month, requesting that the trial start again from scratch.
Berlusconi, who denies charges of complicity in payment of alleged bribes by four companies in his Fininvest business empire, alleged Crivelli was actively siding with prosecutors.

He based his suit on a private exchange between Crivelli and prosecutor Gherardo Colombo in which Crivelli spoke of a "carrot and stick". The conversation, which took place outside formal proceedings, was picked up on court microphones and transcribed.

Amodio said at the time that Crivelli's recorded remarks cast serious doubt on his impartiality. But Crivelli told the court last month the remarks had been a reminder to Colombo that he intended to strike a balance between prosecution and defence.

Berlusconi, prime minister for seven months in 1994, is accused of having conspired in the payment of bribes of 380 million lire ($250,300) to tax police by four of his companies for lenient audits between 1989 and 1991.

The media tycoon, who leads the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, denies knowledge of the payments at the time they were made, argues they were extorted from his group by tax police and says the case is part of a political plot to ruin him. ($1=1518 Lire)
